paragraphs: The trial of Dmitri Karamazov opened in our district court at ten o’clock the next morning, the day after the events I have just described.

Let me say right away that I don’t think I can report everything that happened at the trial in full detail, or even in the order it happened. To mention everything and explain it properly would, I imagine, fill a book, and a very large one. So I hope no one will blame me for sticking to what struck me. I may have picked out as most interesting something that was really of secondary importance, and I may have left out the most prominent and essential points. But I see that I had better not apologize. I will do my best, and the reader will see for himself that I have done all I could.

First, before we go into the courtroom, I want to mention what surprised me most that day. As it turned out, it surprised everyone else too. We all knew the case had stirred up great interest. We knew everybody was burning with impatience for the trial to start, and that local society had talked, guessed, exclaimed and speculated about it for the past two months. We also knew the case was now famous across Russia. Still, we had not imagined that it had roused such fierce, such intense interest in everyone, and not only here but all over Russia. That became obvious at the trial that day.

Visitors had come not just from the chief town of our province but from several other Russian towns, and from Moscow and Petersburg too. There were lawyers among them, and ladies, and even several distinguished personages. Every admission ticket had been snapped up. Behind the table where the three judges sat, a special area was kept for the most distinguished and important of the men. A row of armchairs stood there, which was out of the ordinary and had never been allowed before. A good part of the public, at least half, was made up of ladies. Lawyers had come from everywhere in such numbers that nobody knew where to put them, since every ticket had long ago been eagerly sought and given out. At the far end of the room, behind the platform, I saw that a partition had been hastily put up, and all these lawyers were let in behind it. They counted themselves lucky to have standing room there, because all the chairs had been taken out to make space. The crowd behind the partition stood through the whole trial, packed in shoulder to shoulder.

Some of the ladies, particularly those from out of town, showed up in the gallery very smartly dressed. But most of them had stopped thinking about clothes at all. Their faces showed a feverish, intense, almost unhealthy curiosity. One odd fact, which many observations confirmed afterwards, was that nearly all the ladies, or at least the vast majority, were on Mitya’s side and wanted him acquitted. This was perhaps mainly because he was known as a conqueror of women’s hearts. People knew that two women who were rivals would take part in the case. One of them, Katerina Ivanovna, was the center of general interest. All kinds of extraordinary stories went around about her, amazing anecdotes about her passion for Mitya in spite of his crime. People especially stressed her pride and her “aristocratic connections” (she had visited hardly anyone in the town). They said she meant to ask the Government for permission to follow the criminal to Siberia and marry him somewhere in the mines. Grushenka’s appearance in court was awaited with just as much impatience. The public looked forward with anxious curiosity to the meeting of the two rivals, the proud aristocratic girl and “the hetaira.” But the ladies of the district knew Grushenka better than they knew Katerina Ivanovna. They had already seen “the woman who ruined Fyodor Pavlovitch and his unhappy son.” Almost every one of them wondered how father and son could be so in love with “such a very common, ordinary Russian girl, who wasn’t even pretty.”

In a word, there was a great deal of talk. I know for a fact that our town saw several serious family quarrels over Mitya. Many ladies fought bitterly with their husbands because they disagreed about the dreadful case. It was only natural that those husbands, far from feeling kindly toward the prisoner, came into court bitterly prejudiced against him. One can say with fair certainty that the men in the audience, as opposed to the women, were set against the prisoner. There were plenty of stern, frowning, even vengeful faces. Mitya had, after all, managed to offend a great many people during his time in the town. Some of the visitors, of course, were in the best of spirits and cared nothing about what happened to Mitya himself. But all of them were interested in the trial, and most of the men were surely hoping to see the criminal convicted. Perhaps the lawyers were the exception, since they were more interested in the legal side of the case than in its moral side.

Everyone was stirred by the presence of the famous lawyer Fetyukovitch. His talent was well known, and it was not the first time he had taken on notorious criminal cases in the provinces. When he defended them, such cases became famous and stayed in people’s memories all over Russia. Stories were told about our prosecutor and the President of the Court as well. It was said that Ippolit Kirillovitch was shaking at the prospect of facing Fetyukovitch, and that the two had been enemies from the very start of their careers in Petersburg. Our prosecutor was a touchy man who always felt that someone in Petersburg had wronged him by not valuing his talents. The Karamazov case excited him keenly, and he even dreamed of rebuilding his sinking fortunes through it. But Fetyukovitch, they said, was the one thing that worried him. These rumors, though, were not quite fair. Our prosecutor was not the sort of man who loses heart when faced with danger. On the contrary, the greater the danger, the more his self-confidence grew. It should be said that he was generally too hasty and morbidly impressionable. He would throw his whole soul into a case and work at it as if his entire fate and fortune hung on the outcome. People in the legal world laughed at this a little, because it was exactly this trait that had made our prosecutor better known than his modest position would lead you to expect. They laughed most of all at his passion for psychology. In my opinion they were wrong, and our prosecutor was, I believe, a man of more depth than people supposed. But his health was delicate, so he had failed to make his mark when his career began, and he had never made up for it since.

As for the President of our Court, I can only say that he was a humane, cultured man who knew the practical side of his work and held progressive views. He was fairly ambitious, but he did not trouble himself much over his future career. The great aim of his life was to be a man of advanced ideas. He also had connections and property. As we found out later, he felt quite strongly about the Karamazov case, but in a social way rather than a personal one. It interested him as a social phenomenon, a thing to be classified, a product of our social conditions and typical of the national character, and so on and so forth. The personal side of the case, its tragic meaning and the people caught up in it, the prisoner included, left him rather indifferent and detached, which was perhaps only fitting.

Long before the judges made their entrance, the courtroom was crammed full and people were spilling out. Ours is the finest hall in the town: roomy, high-ceilinged, and good for sound. The judges sat on a raised platform. On their right, a table and two rows of chairs stood ready for the jury. On the left was the place for the prisoner and his defense lawyer. In the middle of the court, close to the judges, stood a table holding the “material proofs.” On it lay Fyodor Pavlovitch’s white silk dressing-gown, stained with blood, and the fatal brass pestle with which the supposed murder was done. There was Mitya’s shirt with one bloodstained sleeve, and his coat, with blood in patches over the pocket where he had put his handkerchief. The handkerchief itself lay there, stiff with blood and by now quite yellow. There was the pistol Mitya had loaded at Perhotin’s with the idea of killing himself, which Trifon Borissovitch had slyly taken from him at Mokroe. There was the envelope in which the three thousand roubles had been put aside for Grushenka, with the narrow pink ribbon it was tied with, and many other things I don’t remember. The seats for the public were farther back, in the main part of the hall. But in front of the balustrade a few chairs had been set out for witnesses who stayed in court once they had given their evidence.

The three judges came in at ten o’clock: the President, an honorary justice of the peace, and one more. The prosecutor naturally entered right behind them. The President was a short, stout, heavily built man of fifty, with a dyspeptic complexion, dark hair going gray and cropped short, and a red ribbon from some Order I can’t remember. The prosecutor looked strikingly pale, almost green, to me and to others as well. His face seemed to have grown thinner all at once, maybe in a single night, since I had seen him looking quite normal only two days earlier. The President opened by asking the court whether the whole jury was there.

But I can see that I can’t keep on like this. Some things I did not hear, some I did not notice, and some I have forgotten. Above all, as I said before, I simply have no time or room to mention everything that was said and done. I only know that neither side challenged many of the jurymen. I remember the twelve: four were small town officials, two were merchants, and six were peasants and artisans from the town. I remember that long before the trial people kept asking, with some surprise, and the ladies most of all: “Can a case this delicate, complex and psychological really be left to petty officials, and even peasants, to decide?” and “What can an official understand about such a matter, let alone a peasant?” All four officials on the jury were in fact insignificant men of low rank. With one younger exception, they were gray-headed men, little known in society, who had withered away on a miserable salary. They probably had elderly, unpresentable wives and swarms of children, perhaps even running around without shoes and stockings. At most they passed their free time over cards, and of course they had never read a single book. The two merchants looked respectable but were oddly silent and stolid. One was clean-shaven and dressed in the European style. The other had a small gray beard and wore a red ribbon around his neck with some kind of medal on it. There is no need to say anything about the artisans and peasants. The artisans of Skotoprigonyevsk are almost peasants, and they even work the land. Two of them also wore European clothes, and maybe that was why they looked dirtier and less appealing than the rest. So one might well wonder, as I did the moment I looked at them, “what could men like that possibly make of such a case?” And yet their faces gave a strangely imposing, almost menacing impression. They were stern and frowning.

At last the President opened the case of the murder of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. I don’t remember exactly how he described him. The court usher was ordered to bring in the prisoner, and Mitya appeared. The court went quiet. You could have heard a fly. I can’t say how it struck others, but Mitya made a very bad impression on me. He looked like a terrible dandy in his brand-new frock-coat. I heard later that he had ordered it from his own tailor in Moscow, who had his measurements, specially for this occasion. He wore flawless black kid gloves and beautiful linen. He strode in with his yard-long steps, looking rigidly straight ahead, and took his seat as calmly as could be.

At that moment Fetyukovitch, the famous counsel for the defense, walked in, and a kind of low murmur went around the court. He was a tall, lean man with long thin legs and very long, thin, pale fingers. His face was clean-shaven, his rather short hair was neatly and primly brushed, and his thin lips sometimes curled into something between a sneer and a smile. He seemed about forty. His face would have been pleasant but for his eyes. They were small and without expression, and they were set remarkably close together, with nothing but his long thin nose between them. In short, there was something strikingly birdlike about his face. He wore evening dress and a white tie.

I remember the President’s first questions to Mitya, about his name, his occupation, and so forth. Mitya replied curtly, in a voice so unexpectedly loud that the President gave a start and looked at the prisoner in surprise. Then a list was read of those who were to take part in the proceedings, meaning the witnesses and the experts. It was a long list. Four of the witnesses were absent. Miüsov, who had testified at the preliminary inquiry, was now in Paris. Madame Hohlakov and Maximov could not come because of illness. Smerdyakov was missing because he had died so suddenly, and an official police statement about it was presented. The news of Smerdyakov’s death caused a sudden stir and whispering in court. Many in the audience, of course, had not heard about the sudden suicide. What struck people most was Mitya’s sudden outburst. The moment the statement about Smerdyakov’s death was made, he shouted out from his seat:
“He was a dog and died like a dog!”

I remember his lawyer rushing over to him, and the President warning him that stern measures would follow if such an outburst were repeated. Mitya nodded, and in a low voice, in abrupt bursts, with no sign of regret, he said several times to his lawyer:
“I won’t again, I won’t. It just came out. I won’t do it again.”

Of course this short episode did him no good with the jury or the public. His character had shown itself, and it spoke for itself. It was right after this incident that the opening statement was read out. It was fairly short but full of detail. It gave only the main reasons why he had been arrested, why he had to be tried, and the like. Even so, it made a great impression on me. The clerk read it loudly and clearly. The whole tragedy was suddenly laid out before us, compressed, in sharp relief, in a fatal and merciless light. I remember that as soon as it had been read, the President asked Mitya, in a loud and solemn voice:
“Prisoner, do you plead guilty?”
Mitya suddenly got to his feet.

“I plead guilty to drunkenness and dissipation,” he cried out, again in a startling, almost frantic voice, “to idleness and debauchery. I meant to become an honest man for good, just at the moment when fate struck me down. But I am not guilty of the death of that old man, my enemy and my father. No, no, I am not guilty of robbing him! I couldn’t be. Dmitri Karamazov is a scoundrel, but he is not a thief.”

He sat down again, plainly shaking all over. The President once more warned him, briefly but forcefully, to answer only what he was asked and not to break out into irrelevant cries. Then he ordered the case to go forward. All the witnesses were brought up to be sworn. That was when I saw them all together. The prisoner’s brothers, though, were allowed to testify without an oath. After a word of exhortation from the priest and the President, the witnesses were led out and seated as far from one another as could be managed. Then they began calling them up one at a time.
